questions.questionText: What is the primary objective of an email phishing attack targeting remote employees?

options.text: To test home internet connection speeds
To trick users into revealing credentials, sensitive data, or executing unauthorized actions
To automatically upgrade operating system software
To clean junk files from a local hard drive

questions.explanation: Email phishing uses deceptive messages to trick victims into sharing private credentials, executing malware, or surrendering sensitive organizational data.

questions.questionText: The presence of "HTTPS" and a padlock icon in the browser address bar guarantees that a login website is legitimate and safe.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Threat actors can easily acquire free SSL/TLS certificates for fraudulent domain names, displaying HTTPS padlock icons on malicious credential-harvesting websites.

questions.questionText: What does the term "Quishing" refer to in modern cybersecurity?

options.text: Sending phishing attempts via voice phone calls
Hacking smart television devices
Using malicious QR codes to conceal phishing URLs and bypass security filters
Encrypting databases using ransomware

questions.explanation: Quishing stands for QR code phishing, where malicious links are embedded in image files to bypass textual email filters.

questions.questionText: Which domain name represents an example of "typosquatting"?

options.text: support.google.com
login.microsoft.com
security-update@micros0ft-verify.com
portal.slack.com

questions.explanation: micros0ft-verify.com uses a zero ('0') in place of the letter 'o' to trick users into believing it is an official Microsoft communication channel.

questions.questionText: Security Email Gateways (SEGs) detect embedded QR code links just as easily as standard plain-text web links.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Traditional SEGs primarily scan textual and HTML links. Image-based QR codes often bypass standard filters because the URL is hidden inside the graphic payload.

questions.questionText: Which of the following indicators strongly suggest that an email may be a phishing attempt? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Mismatch between the display sender name and the actual email domain address
Messages requesting urgent multi-factor authentication (MFA) re-verification
Digitally signed calendar invites sent from verified internal team accounts
Unsolicited attachments asking you to enable macros to view content

questions.explanation: Mismatched headers, urgent MFA prompts, and macro-enabled attachments are classic phishing indicators. Digitally signed internal calendar invites are standard workflow items.

questions.questionText: You receive an email from IT-Support@company-desk.net stating: "Your password expires in 10 minutes. Click here to retain your current password." What should you do first?

options.text: Click the link immediately to prevent losing account access
Forward the email to your personal account so you don't lose the link
Pause, do not click the link, and verify the sender address against official internal IT contacts
Reply to the email providing your current password so IT can fix it for you

questions.explanation: You should pause and verify unrequested urgent security alerts independently through official internal channels.

questions.questionText: Why do quishing attacks often succeed when targeting remote employees?

options.text: Smartphones cannot connect to Wi-Fi networks
Scanning the QR code shifts the browsing session to a mobile device outside the company's desktop security monitoring
QR codes automatically disable smartphone antivirus apps
Mobile screens automatically encrypt all user passwords

questions.explanation: Scanning QR codes on personal phones redirects traffic outside the desktop perimeter firewalls and email monitoring systems maintained by corporate networks.

questions.questionText: Hovering your mouse over a hyperlinked button in an email allows you to preview the actual destination URL before clicking.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Hovering over a hyperlink reveals the true underlying web destination address in the browser or mail client status bar.

questions.questionText: Which of the following file extensions attached to an unsolicited email should be treated as high-risk? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: .pdf.exe
.docm (Macro-enabled Word document)
.png
.vbs (Visual Basic Script)

questions.explanation: Double extensions (.pdf.exe), macro-enabled documents (.docm), and script files (.vbs) can automatically execute malicious payloads on a host computer.

questions.questionText: A remote freelancer receives an email with an embedded QR code labeled "Scan to View Signed Client NDA." Scans show the QR code opens http://192.168.1.1/login.html. Is this safe to open?

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Legitimate signed contracts are not hosted on raw local IP addresses or delivered via unencrypted QR codes without prior client agreement.

questions.questionText: What is the safest way to access a company cloud portal after receiving a suspicious email notification?

options.text: Click the link in the email, enter credentials, then log out
Open a fresh browser tab, type the verified official URL manually or use a saved bookmark
Reply to the email asking if the link is safe
Copy and paste the link into a personal social media post to ask colleagues

questions.explanation: Navigating independently via a trusted bookmark or manual URL entry completely bypasses any malicious redirects embedded in the email.

questions.questionText: Combosquatting involves adding words like "-security" or "-login" to legitimate brand names within a domain registration.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Combosquatting merges legitimate brand trademarks with keywords (e.g., paypal-update-center.com) to mislead recipients.

questions.questionText: A virtual assistant receives an email displaying the company CEO’s exact name and profile photo. The sender address is ceo-office@exec-mail-corp.com (not the corporate @company.com domain). The message requests an urgent purchase of gift card vouchers for an ongoing client event. What social engineering tactic is being deployed?

options.text: Mass Ransomware Distribution
Executive Spoofing via Combosquatting Phishing
Authorized Corporate Expense Request
Automated Database Synchronization

questions.explanation: The attacker uses executive identity impersonation combined with a combosquatted external domain (exec-mail-corp.com) to trick the assistant into making unauthorized purchases.

questions.questionText: What technical security mechanisms can organizations configure to help block spoofed email headers? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: SPF (Sender Policy Framework)
DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)
DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance)
Upgrading physical monitor screen resolutions

questions.explanation: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are DNS-based email authentication protocols configured to verify sender domain legitimacy and stop header spoofing.

questions.questionText: You scan a QR code from a vendor PDF. It opens a Google Sign-In page asking you to "Grant Full OAuth Permissions to App XYZ." Granting access is safe because the URL starts with accounts.google.com.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Malicious OAuth applications use real Google/Microsoft sign-in portals to request excessive account permissions. Once granted, the attacker gets persistent cloud access without needing your password.

questions.questionText: What is the primary reason threat actors exploit human curiosity or urgency during a phishing attempt?

options.text: To test the bandwidth limitations of home routers
To trigger fast, emotional decision-making that bypasses logical identity verification
To force web browsers to automatically clear local cache files
To shorten the length of domain URLs

questions.explanation: High-pressure emotional triggers (fear, urgency, curiosity) induce cognitive overload, causing targets to act before inspecting sender details or verifying requests.

questions.questionText: A remote software engineer receives an email containing a link to a "Critical Security Patch" hosted on github-downloads-security.net. What is the most rigorous way to confirm if this patch is legitimate?

options.text: Click the link, download the file, and scan it with a free online tool
Check official internal engineering channels (e.g., internal Slack/Teams or company repo) and consult the lead system administrator
Forward the email to external contacts on LinkedIn to ask if they received it
Reply directly asking the sender for their corporate employee ID number

questions.explanation: Internal verification via official out-of-band communication channels is the only reliable way to confirm patch validity.

questions.questionText: If you realize you entered your corporate credentials into a fake login portal 5 minutes ago, what immediate steps must you execute? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Change the password immediately across your corporate account and any accounts reusing that password
Revoke active user sessions and alert your organization’s IT/Security team
Delete your browser history and turn off your home router for 24 hours
Check active multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices registered to your account for unauthorized additions

questions.explanation: Resetting credentials, revoking active sessions, alerting IT, and auditing registered MFA devices stops ongoing unauthorized account access. Deleting local browser history does not stop the remote attacker.

questions.questionText: Phishing attacks targeting remote employees exclusively occur through traditional business email, never through personal email or instant messaging platforms.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Attackers routinely target remote employees across personal email, LinkedIn DMs, WhatsApp, and Telegram to bypass enterprise email controls. MODULE 2: Spear Phishing
